passage: Instructor's note, statistics bridge course, 4 May. Written by Vaibhav. Indu, nineteen, one of three women in a section of forty, came to my office before the midterm. She said she had heard for years that girls "don't have the head for numbers," and that before tests her hands shook. We talked through what she already does. She now writes one line at the top of every paper: "This shows what I've practised, not what I'm worth." She keeps a list of problems she once couldn't do and now can. She has also joined the Thursday study circle run by a final-year student who, in her words, "actually expects me to get it." On my side, I have stopped calling the midterm a test of ability. I now tell the class it is a checkpoint that shows us what to practise next. Indu's score rose from 54 to 71.

qa.q: What line does Indu write at the top of every paper?
qa.a: "This shows what I've practised, not what I'm worth."

qa.q: What did Indu feel before tests, and what lay behind it?
qa.a: Her hands shook before tests, because she had heard for years that girls don't have the head for numbers.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav change on the instructor's side, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Vaibhav stopped calling the midterm a test of ability and called it a checkpoint for what to practise next, which removes the sense of a verdict.

qa.q: How might the final-year student who runs the study circle affect Indu?
qa.a: By expecting Indu to get it, that student gives her someone who believes in her, which counters the old label.

grounding: A student reframes tests as measures of practice, recalls her progress and seeks a believing mentor, while her instructor frames the midterm as a step in growth.

passage: Wednesday night. Big accounts exam tomorrow, and the old voice is back: "People from our village don't pass these exams in one go." Uncle said it at the wedding as if he were talking about the weather. My stomach's been tight since dinner. So I did what Farhan told me to try. First, I wrote on a card: This exam checks my preparation. It does not measure me. Second, I listed three hard things I've already done: topped the district in Class 12, taught myself spreadsheets, and passed first year despite the flood. Third, I wrote why I'm doing this: so Amma never has to borrow before the harvest again. Then I messaged Farhan, who passed last year. Reply: "You're ready. You know the ledger chapter better than I did." Card's in my pencil box. Going to sleep. - Ganga

qa.q: What did Ganga write on the card?
qa.a: This exam checks my preparation. It does not measure me.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling after dinner, and what set it off?
qa.a: Ganga felt anxious, with a tight stomach since dinner, because Uncle's remark that people from their village don't pass these exams in one go had come back.

qa.q: Which of Ganga's steps seems most useful the night before the exam, and why?
qa.a: Listing three hard things already done, like topping the district, because it sets real evidence of ability against Uncle's label.

qa.q: How might Farhan's reply affect Ganga's night?
qa.a: Hearing from someone who passed last year that Ganga is ready gives belief from someone who has been through it, which may make sleep and the morning easier.

grounding: A student facing a group label reminds themselves that the exam measures preparation, recalls past successes and values, and turns to someone who passed before and believes in them.

passage:
The polytechnic in Chitradurga had one drawing hall with slow fans and forty slanted desks. The night before the engineering drawing exam, Lakshmi, nineteen, heard it again from her uncle on the phone: "Girls from the village can't see in 3D. Don't feel bad if you fail."
She lay on the hostel cot with a tight stomach. Then she sat up and wrote three lines in her notebook. This test measures practice, not my worth. I drew the old fort gate from memory in Class 9 and won the district prize. I want to build bridges for my village.
In the morning she stopped at Vinita Ma'am's cabin. "Ma'am, am I ready?"
Vinita looked through her practice sheets. "These say yes. Think of the exam as one more sheet, a chance to see what you've learned, not a verdict on you."
Lakshmi walked into the hall and sharpened her pencil twice, slowly.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi draw from memory in Class 9?
qa.a: The old fort gate, which won the district prize.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi write three lines in her notebook the night before?
qa.a: She was anxious after her uncle's remark and wanted to remind herself of her worth, her past success and what she values.

qa.q: How did Vinita Ma'am's framing of the exam help?
qa.a: Calling it one more sheet to see what she had learned, not a verdict, eased the threat so Lakshmi could focus.

qa.q: How might the uncle see his remark compared with how it landed for Lakshmi?
qa.a: He may have meant to comfort her in advance, but it planted the very doubt she had to work to push away.

grounding: A student under a group stereotype reminds herself the test measures practice, recalls past success and values, and a mentor frames the exam as growth, not a verdict.

passage:
Emil, twenty, had come to the university in Copenhagen from a vocational college, where he had spent two years fixing ship engines. In the first week of linear algebra a classmate joked, "Mechanics take this course twice, right?" Emil laughed, then felt his neck go hot every time a quiz came round.
Before Friday's quiz he walked to the harbour and made himself remember: the engine he had rebuilt after the certified man gave up; why he wanted this degree, to design quieter ferries. A quiz measures what I've practised, he told himself. Not who I am.
In class Dr Priscila Santos handed out the sheets. "This is a map, not a grade. It shows us both what to work on next." Afterwards she sat beside him and went through his two mistakes as if they were interesting.
Emil folded the sheet into his pocket. For once it felt like information.

qa.q: What had Emil spent two years fixing at the vocational college?
qa.a: Ship engines.

qa.q: Why did Emil walk to the harbour before Friday's quiz?
qa.a: He wanted to calm the hot-necked fear by reminding himself of his past success and why he wanted the degree.

qa.q: What did Dr Santos do that reduced the threat for Emil?
qa.a: She framed the quiz as a map for growth, not a grade, and treated his mistakes as interesting rather than as proof of anything.

qa.q: What would change for Emil if the quiz were framed as a verdict on ability?
qa.a: His neck would likely go hot again, and the fear of confirming the classmate's joke could crowd out his real skill.

grounding: A student reminds himself a quiz measures practice not worth and recalls past success and values, while an instructor frames the quiz as a map for growth.

passage: Ten minutes before the electronics exam at the engineering college in Coimbatore, Keerthana stood outside the hall. She was one of four girls in a batch of sixty, and she'd heard the old joke again at breakfast: girls in core branches are only there for the reservation seats. Her chest was tight. She closed her eyes and did what Pema ma'am, her faculty mentor, had taught her: name three things. One, this test measures what I've prepared, not what I'm worth. Two, I built a working amplifier in second year that nobody else could. Three, I'm here because I love figuring out circuits. She breathed out. Inside, Pema ma'am had written on the board: "Today is a checkpoint, not a verdict. Show me where you are." Keerthana sat down and read the first question slowly. She knew it.

qa.q: How many girls were in Keerthana's batch?
qa.a: She was one of four girls in a batch of sixty.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling outside the hall, and how did it change?
qa.a: Keerthana felt tense, chest tight from the joke, then calmer after reminding herself of her preparation and past success.

qa.q: How did Pema ma'am's board message help the students?
qa.a: Framing the exam as a checkpoint, not a verdict, lowers the stakes and helps students like Keerthana focus on the problems instead of the threat.

qa.q: How might the other girls in the batch feel reading Pema ma'am's message?
qa.a: They might feel relieved and supported, knowing their mentor sees the exam as a step in growth rather than a judgement of their worth.

grounding: A student reminds herself a test measures preparation, recalls past success and values, and is helped by a mentor who frames the exam as growth, not a verdict.

passage:
Dear Tashi didi,
You won't remember me, but you gave a talk at our hostel last year about being the first person from your village to finish a law degree. I'm writing because of the thing you said: "Tests measure preparation, not your worth."
I'm in my second year of statistics. When I joined, a senior told me students from small-town schools always struggle here. Before every exam I'd feel sick, and my scores were worse than my homework.
This term I tried your method. Before each test I wrote in my notebook: I've studied chapters four to seven. I topped my district in class twelve. I chose this because I love numbers. It sounds silly. It worked. I also asked Professor Nair to be my mentor. She said she already believed in me and wanted to see me grow, not prove anything.
Thank you.
Gurleen

qa.q: Which chapters did Gurleen write down as studied?
qa.a: Gurleen wrote, "I've studied chapters four to seven."

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel before exams in the first year?
qa.a: Gurleen felt sick and anxious, carrying the senior's claim that small-town students struggle.

qa.q: Which part of Gurleen's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Writing down preparation, past success and love of numbers before each test, and finding a mentor who believes in growth, eased the pressure so exam scores could match the homework.

qa.q: How might Tashi didi feel receiving this letter?
qa.a: Tashi didi would likely feel moved and proud that one line from the talk helped a student she never met.

grounding: A student uses reminders of preparation, past successes and values, and a believing mentor, to reduce the threat of a label about small-town students.

I'm Shreya. I sat next to Nitin in the physics tutorial all year, so I saw this, though I can't say what went on in his head.
Nitin was from a rural school, and some classmates joked that "village boys can't handle theory." Before the first mid-semester exam, his hands shook.

He also started staying after class with Professor Das, who told the whole group, "Exams show what we need to work on, not who we are."
Nitin's marks rose steadily. He still gets nervous. But he doesn't shake any more.

passage: The exam centre changed at the last minute, and Sarika spent forty minutes in an auto crawling through Hyderabad traffic, heart pounding. So she did what her mentor, Kalyani Ma'am, had taught her. She took out the index card from her bag and read it: 'This test shows how I prepared, not what I'm worth. I have prepared.' On the back, in her own handwriting: the hackathon she won, the scholarship, and 'I love this work.' She breathed slowly for ten counts. Her phone buzzed: Kalyani Ma'am. 'Go show them what you showed me.' Sarika switched it off, walked in, and read the first question once.

qa.q: What was written on the front of Sarika's index card?
qa.a: 'This test shows how I prepared, not what I'm worth. I have prepared.'

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling in the queue?
qa.a: Sarika felt anxious, the old knot of fear about what people said about her college.

qa.q: Why do the index card and the breathing help?
qa.a: They shift Sarika's focus from the label to her real preparation, past successes and love of the work, freeing her mind for the questions.

qa.q: What might Kalyani Ma'am's message mean to Sarika?

grounding: Under last-minute pressure a student reframes an entrance test as a measure of preparation, recalls successes and leans on a mentor's belief.

passage: Alka was the first in her family to go to college, and in the Kolkata statistics class she felt it: the others had tutors, laptops, parents who explained things at dinner. Before the first quiz her hands went cold. Then Kishore Sir, the instructor, did something unusual. He wrote on the board: 'This quiz is a map, not a verdict. It shows what to practise next.' He added that nobody's marks would be read aloud, and that everyone would get a second attempt after a practice week. Alka felt her shoulders drop an inch. That evening she wrote on a sticky note by her bed: 'Scholarship. Topped Class 12 in my district. I'm here because I earned it.' In the second attempt she scored eighteen out of twenty. She sent a photo to her mother, who couldn't read English but understood the number.

qa.q: What did Kishore Sir write on the board?
qa.a: 'This quiz is a map, not a verdict. It shows what to practise next.'

qa.q: What did Alka feel when Kishore Sir explained the quiz?
qa.a: Alka felt relieved, her shoulders dropping an inch as the pressure eased.

qa.q: What did Alka add herself to reduce the threat?
qa.a: A sticky note listing her scholarship and district topping, reminding her she earned her place.

qa.q: How might Alka's mother feel seeing the photo?
qa.a: Her mother would likely feel proud and joyful, understanding the number even without reading English.

grounding: An instructor frames a quiz as growth, not a verdict, and a first-generation student adds her own reminders of past success.

'I can't go up there,' Shankar whispered, clutching his slides outside the seminar hall. 'Every other speaker is from the big national institutes. They'll think the state university kid copied something.'
'Did you copy something?' Irawati asked.
'No! I built the whole model.'
'Then what is the talk for?'
'To... show the model.'
'To show what you learned. Not whether you deserve to be here. You were already selected.' She held up three fingers. 'Tell me three things you've done that you're proud of.'
He thought. 'The monsoon data set. The poster prize. Teaching the juniors to code.'
'Good. Say them in your head when you walk up. And look at me in the third row. I'll be nodding like an idiot.'
Shankar laughed shakily. 'You'd better.'
'I believe in your model. Go.'

qa.q: What did Shankar build?
qa.a: The whole model.

qa.q: What is Shankar afraid of before his talk?
qa.a: Shankar is anxious that the others will assume a state university student copied the work.

qa.q: What did Irawati do to reduce the threat?
qa.a: She reframed the talk as showing what he learned, had him recall three proud successes, and promised visible belief from the third row.

qa.q: How does Irawati see Shankar's work?
qa.a: Irawati believes in his model and sees him as fully deserving his place.

grounding: A mentor helps a student fearing a group stereotype reframe his talk, recall past successes and feel believed in.
